title: USS Lincoln Returns to San Diego Bay After Historic Long‑Term Deployment – AP News
body:
Sailors from the nuclear‑powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln stepped onto the dock at Naval Base San Diego on Thursday, ending a historic 265‑day uninterrupted deployment that kept the warship at sea for nearly nine months while it supported operations against Iran. The arrival was marked by a modest ceremony, but the significance of the mission – the longest continuous sea stint for a U.S. carrier in more than a decade – resonated through the ranks of the crew, the Navy’s leadership, and the broader public, which has followed the carrier’s grueling schedule and the mounting reports of fatigue, supply shortages and mental‑health strain among its sailors.

The carrier, which left San Diego in early March, spent the bulk of its time in the Arabian Sea and the Persian Gulf, launching air strikes, providing air‑cover for maritime patrols and serving as a floating command center for coalition forces. Its air wing flew more than 7,000 sorties, delivering precision munitions against Iranian‑backed militia targets and protecting commercial shipping lanes from missile attacks. The extended presence was intended to deter further escalation after Tehran’s recent missile launches and to reassure allies in the region, a goal that senior defense officials say was largely achieved.

However, the unprecedented length of the deployment exposed systemic challenges in sustaining crew welfare on long‑range operations. Navy reports released in the weeks leading up to the ship’s return highlighted a surge in mental‑health consultations, increased incidents of sleep deprivation, and shortages of basic supplies such as fresh food and laundry services. Some sailors described the conditions as “a test of endurance,” while others voiced concerns that the operational tempo left little room for rest or family contact. The Navy’s leadership has pledged to review the deployment schedule, improve logistical pipelines, and expand onboard counseling resources to mitigate the risks of burnout in future extended missions.

The homecoming also sparked a broader debate about the United States’ reliance on carrier strike groups as the backbone of its power‑projection strategy. Critics argue that the high cost of maintaining a carrier fleet—both in terms of dollars and human capital—necessitates a reevaluation of how and when such assets are employed. Proponents counter that the Lincoln’s sustained presence helped prevent a wider regional conflict and demonstrated the Navy’s ability to project force far from American shores. As the Pentagon continues to balance fiscal constraints with strategic imperatives, the Lincoln’s deployment may serve as a case study for calibrating future carrier use, especially as newer classes of ships and unmanned systems enter service.

For the crew members disembarking, the transition back to shore life will be gradual. Many will receive medical and psychological evaluations, and a portion of the ship’s personnel will be rotated to other vessels or shore assignments to allow for recovery. Families who have awaited their loved ones’ return expressed relief and pride, while also acknowledging the challenges ahead in reintegrating after such a prolonged separation. The Navy has arranged a series of support events, including counseling sessions and community gatherings, to ease the adjustment.

Looking ahead, the USS Abraham Lincoln is slated for a comprehensive maintenance period at the shipyard, during which it will undergo upgrades to its radar, communications suite and aircraft handling systems. The overhaul is expected to keep the carrier operationally ready for the next cycle of deployments, which analysts predict will focus on the Indo‑Pacific theater amid rising tensions with China. The lessons learned from this record‑breaking stint—particularly regarding crew resilience and logistical sustainment—are likely to shape policy decisions as the Navy strives to balance global commitments with the wellbeing of its sailors.
